plan.chapterName: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 10: Liquids and Solids
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single energy-level schematic relating the enthalpy changes of the phase transitions among three states of matter. A black vertical arrow along the left edge, labeled Energy, points upward and sets the vertical scale; no numerical values appear anywhere. Three horizontal blue lines cross the diagram at increasing heights, labeled at their right-hand ends Solid at the bottom, Liquid about a third of the way up, and Gas near the top, with the solid-to-liquid separation noticeably smaller than the liquid-to-gas separation. Three thick red arrows point upward between these levels. The leftmost spans the full distance from the Solid line to the Gas line and is labeled Sublimation, delta H sub. Just to its right a shorter arrow rises only from the Solid line to the Liquid line, labeled Fusion, delta H fus, and directly above that arrow a third one continues from the Liquid line to the Gas line, labeled Vaporization, delta H vap. Placing the one long arrow beside two stacked shorter arrows that together cover the same vertical distance lets the additive relation among the three quantities be read straight off the drawing. The layout supports modeling sublimation as melting followed by vaporization so that the enthalpies of the individual steps can be summed.

interactionPlan.concept: The enthalpy change for sublimation equals the sum of the enthalpies of fusion and vaporization, because enthalpy depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken.

interactions.label: Step the phase path
interactions.teaches: Melting and then boiling carries the sample from the Solid level to the Gas level in two additive energy steps, and the running total ends at exactly the Gas line.

interactions.label: Route from solid to gas
interactions.teaches: The same initial and final states can be reached directly or in two steps, and the total vertical rise — the enthalpy change — is identical either way.

demo_steps.title: Three energy levels
demo_steps.narration: Three blue lines mark the relative enthalpy of solid, liquid and gas for the same substance. Higher line means higher energy; the liquid-to-gas gap is much larger than the solid-to-liquid gap.

demo_steps.title: The direct route: sublimation
demo_steps.narration: One long red arrow takes the solid straight to the gas. Its length is ΔH_sub, the energy that must be absorbed for sublimation.

demo_steps.title: Step 1 — melting
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the two-step route and add ΔH_fus: the sample climbs only from the Solid line to the Liquid line, and the running total on the right rises by that short amount.

demo_steps.title: Step 2 — vaporizing
demo_steps.narration: Adding ΔH_vap lifts the liquid the rest of the way to the Gas line. The running total now sits exactly at the top of the sublimation arrow.

demo_steps.title: Both routes, same height
demo_steps.narration: Show the long arrow beside the two stacked arrows: they end at the same level, so ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap. Enthalpy is a state function — the path does not matter.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Two stacked arrows reach exactly the same height as the single long arrow, so the enthalpy of sublimation is just melting plus boiling added together — enthalpy depends only on the start and end states.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: White background, landscape layout. Left edge: a thin black arrow pointing up with the bold vertical word 'Energy'; no numbers or tick marks anywhere. Three thick horizontal royal-blue lines span most of the width: 'Solid' low, 'Liquid' at roughly one third height, 'Gas' near the top, each label in plain black text just outside the right end of its line (Gas and Liquid above their lines, Solid below). The Liquid-to-Gas span should be about twice the Solid-to-Liquid span. Two vertical columns of thick dark-red (firebrick) arrows with solid triangular heads sit in the middle-left area: the left column is one arrow from Solid to Gas labeled 'Sublimation / ΔH_sub' (text to its left, in the lower band); the right column is a short arrow Solid→Liquid labeled 'Fusion / ΔH_fus' to its right in the lower band, plus an arrow Liquid→Gas labeled 'Vaporization / ΔH_vap' to its right in the upper band. Inactive arrows in a view should fade to light gray rather than disappear, so the comparison stays legible. During the stepped sequence, highlight the active arrow (brighter red, slight glow) and grow a slim vertical running-total bar along the far right from the Solid level up to the current state, capped by a small horizontal tick; when it reaches Gas, draw a dashed gray horizontal line across to the top of the sublimation arrow and show the annotation 'ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap' in the upper-left whitespace.

authoredContext:
Consider the extent to which intermolecular attractions must be overcome to achieve a given phase transition. Converting a solid into a liquid requires that these attractions be only partially overcome; transition to the gaseous state requires that they be completely overcome. As a result, the enthalpy of fusion for a substance is less than its enthalpy of vaporization. This same logic can be used to derive an approximate relation between the enthalpies of all phase changes for a given substance. Though not an entirely accurate description, sublimation may be conveniently modeled as a sequential two-step process of melting followed by vaporization in order to apply Hess’s Law. Viewed in this manner, the enthalpy of sublimation for a substance may be estimated as the sum of its enthalpies of fusion and vaporization, as illustrated in the figure. For example:

For a given substance, the sum of its enthalpy of fusion and enthalpy of vaporization is approximately equal to its enthalpy of sublimation.

A diagram is shown with a vertical line drawn on the left side and labeled “Energy” and three horizontal lines drawn near the bottom, lower third and top of the diagram. These three lines are labeled, from bottom to top, “Solid,” “Liquid” and “Gas.” Near the middle of the diagram, a vertical, upward-facing arrow is drawn from the solid line to the gas line and labeled “Sublimation, delta sign, H, subscript sub.” To the right of this arrow is a second vertical, upward-facing arrow that is drawn from the solid line to the liquid line and labeled “Fusion, delta sign, H, subscript fus.” Above the second arrow is a third arrow drawn from the liquid line to the gas line and labeled, “Vaporization, delta sign, H, subscript vap.”
